title: Notes of Ministry - 76 - March 1979

paragraphs.text: Our brother’s reference to encouragement encourages me to say a word, and I might say that during the past week or so we have been greatly encouraged by what we have observed amongst the saints, the quality of the work of God in them. The saints are great as being “in Christ”, but then also as having certain moral features that the Lord names and commends. It has really been a great stimulation to be amongst the saints and to observe these qualities. I think we might as well face the fact that there are grades of quality. It is not to exclude any true believers, but the Lord has a right to commend those He approves, and we would wish to be among them. Paul says, “For not he that commends himself is approved, but wham the Lord commends”, 2 Corinthians 10: 18.

What marks these beloved women in Matthew 28 is obedience. The Lord had told them through the angel, “Go quickly and say to his disciples that he is risen from the dead”. Then it says, “And as they went to bring his disciples word, behold also, Jesus met them, saying, Hail!”. How wonderful that is, that Jesus should say “Hail!” to them! We speak humbly of these things, and yet it is right that we should enjoy what belongs to us; without assuming anything, but the Lord evidently greatly values obedience. What generally marks that which professes His name publicly, alas; is not obedience. But there are some who are obedient, and we want to be among them. It is the basis of the fellowship that we are obedient in relation to the lordship of Christ.

“Jesus met them, saying, Hail!”—you can hardly take it in that He would so speak to His own and dignify them thus. I think He would say that to us as we come together in obedience and dependence on the Holy Spirit. He would greet us as we come together as being great persons spiritually, because if the Spirit has worked in us there is a quality that is going through, but shines now, and that the Lord can recognise.

So in Revelation 3 the Lord says that He has certain ones in Sardis that have not defiled their garments. He takes account of that—“Thou hast a few names in Sardis which have not defiled their garments”. So it is not a matter of numbers now, but of quality, and the more you insist on quality the less numbers you may have. In any product or merchandise quality certainly requires reduction in quantity—not that we want numbers reduced, for numbers in relation to the things of God are valuable too. So the Lord says, “Those thou hast given me I have guarded, and not one of them has perished, but the son of perdition”, John 17: 12. Then He repeats it when He protects His own in John 18: 9, “I have not lost one of them”. These were prophetic statements by the Lord.

Here in Revelation 3 He is speaking about His people, “Thou hast a few names in Sardis ...”—“names” is fine! They are personalities, individual personalities that the Lord would take account of, each one, as if He would say, ‘I can tell you the names if you wish’. And they have not defiled their garments. It is sometimes said that we must not be negative. I know what is meant, and agree with it too, but the Lord speaks of what they have not done; they have not defiled their garments. So He values what we do not do. There are a lot of things we do not do, and cannot do, and the Lord takes account of all that.

Then He adds, “They shall walk with me in, white, because they are worthy”. Think of the Lord saying that—“They are worthy”! It is His assessment; they are worthy persons, and they are going to have their reward. Their reward is mentioned in all these words, to the assemblies. These are the Lord’s own words; it is very impressive. They will be associated with Him, those that He approves, the overcomers. So the Lord says of these, “They shall walk with me in white, because they are worthy”. Well, we could not look for anything better than that, could we? He recognises that they had not defiled their garments, and that will then be in evidence, it will be displayed.

I think these scriptures make it all worth while. There are testings, as to the matter of separation but the Lord would attach this name “worthy” to such as accept them. In Revelation 5 the universe is searched to find someone worthy to open the book, and there was not anybody found worthy—but He was worthy, and He is saying of these few persons in Sardis, “They shall walk with me in white, because they are worthy”. That is not only sovereignty; it is a moral basis for the Lord’s approval, and what a privilege it is, beloved brethren, individually and collectively, to supply the Lord with a moral basis for that to which He can apply this wonderful adjective “worthy”.

Then to Philadelphia the Lord says, “I will cause that they shall come and shall do homage before thy feet, and shall know that I have loved thee”. So what a matter that is, beloved brethren—of this time, when we are despised and unknown, the Lord is going to say in that day, ‘While you looked down on these brethren and despised what they were going on

with in their meetings, I was loving them’. It does not say here, as in chapter 1, ‘Him who loves us’; that is present; but ‘I have loved thee’. How precious that is! What an encouragement, too, to continue maintaining His things, as He says of Philadelphia, “Because thou hast kept the word of my patience”. This word “because” is very important. It is not an abstract matter; there are moral grounds for what the Lord says. How He values that! Then the promise, “I also will keep thee out of the hour of trial, which is about to come upon the whole habitable world, to try them that dwell upon the earth”. What a comforting thought that is as we can see such awful conditions arising and moving quickly towards their terrible terminus. He says, “Because thou hast kept the word of my patience”; that is to be noted; we need to have patience. He is coming, and we are to be sensitive and ready for His quick movements. In the gospel of Luke there are various allusions to what is done suddenly. We need to be sensitive—not merely orthodox or to get into a rut—but to be ready for the Lord moving quickly, and to be expecting Him.

Well, dear brethren, that is what I had in mind for our encouragement. Our ministry meetings are not for correction only, but for “edification, and encouragement, and consolation”, 1 Corinthians 14: 3.

We live in the greatest conceivable days. This time of the Spirit brings out the divine glory in the richest and most fruitful way. There has been no time like this time, nor will there ever be another time like it; it will be understood that I am speaking not just of the present immediate period, but of the immensity of the Spirit’s day, this time which began at Pentecost when the Spirit came, and continues till the Lord comes to take His lovers to be with Him. It is a time which lovers of Christ rejoicingly recognise to be in its very last moments before its triumphal conclusion, when the Lord comes and takes all that are His to be with Himself—when, as it says so feelingly in the scripture, “we shall be always with the Lord”, 1 Thessalonians 4: 17.

Now I believe the case of Saul of Tarsus, of whose initial touch of blessing we have read, is to set out the prime example of what God is able for in this time. That is peculiarly vital to what enters into the present moment, to see what God is able to do in respect of man. This was a singularly significant time in the course of God’s testimony; the Spirit had come at Pentecost, believers had been secured, and the testimony had taken a certain course, particularly in Jerusalem. Now God is widening out the great scene of His testimony. There were the crowds at the beginning, at Jerusalem; there were the thousands at the start; but now God is embarking upon the richest and most fruitful line of activity which enters into the testimony. He secures in the

first instance one man. No doubt there were many others brought in in one way and another, but the point I am calling attention to is that the Spirit focuses attention on this one man, as if He would show us what God is able for in one man. He changed the man to bring him into full, sympathetic, energetic support of what He brought forward in His movements.
Saul of Tarsus was embarked on a murderous course against lovers of Christ, as it says,

“breathing out threatenings and slaughter”, Acts 9: 1. I doubt not there were those who wondered just how they could check what this evil man was doing. The Lord shows that He can check this man in what he is doing, but He can do far, far more; He can establish His thoughts in this man; He turns him right round. The Lord does not act in judgment in respect of him; He changes the man right round and makes him for the time His leading servant, the great apostle of the gentiles. That is the mark of this time of the Spirit, in which the Lord Jesus is on high; that same glorious Lord Jesus comes out of heaven to secure this man, to turn him right round, to make him indeed His faithful and most distinctive servant of the time. Think of God being able for that! If He is able for it for one, He is able for it for everyone; but God is not choosing at this point to bring out His work in great numbers. What He does elect to do is to bring out His work in its own choice, distinctive character, showing its refinement. We all know some at least of the details of the history of this man that show how his change was complete.

No, there was never a time like this. God wrought in times beforehand; God wrought in Abraham, in Sarah, in David, and in Solomon, but there was never a case like this; it is glorious in the way in which God intervenes, not only to stop the various activities of opposition upon which Saul of Tarsus was embarked, and to meet all that underlay that in this man’s soul, but in changing him round to become the greatest exponent for the time of the precious truth of God, the precious truth especially of the mystery of Christ and the assembly. There never was, prior to this, a time in which the testimony stood related to Christ in glory. I wonder if the blessedness of that has really claimed our attention, the blessedness of the testimony of a glorified Christ. Christ is out of death, the whole power of death met and overcome, and He has gone into a place of pre-eminence at the right hand of God; He has gone to the Father, to the place of love; Christ is up there and the Holy Spirit is here. In due time we see how Paul comes into the circle of lovers of Christ, and finds the Spirit as he comes among them; he finds one who comes to him and by whose hands, under God’s wise directing touch, he receives the Spirit.

Let us think about receiving the Spirit. Let us go back to the time when we were conscious that we received the Spirit. What a remarkable gift—which is the mark peculiarly of this time of which we are speaking—the gift of the Holy Spirit, giving us objectives outside everything here, giving us indeed a single glorious Objective in Christ in glory. The Spirit makes Christ in glory a centre for our affections, a governing point for our lives in their entirety; He speaks to us about Christ and makes Him precious to our hearts. He speaks in the simplest tones to the dear young people who are believers in the Lord Jesus and have obeyed Him and received the Holy Spirit; they find that the Spirit is able to tell them about Jesus, not only as He was, but Jesus as He is. This gives us, in the glorified Man, a centre of affection, a centre of interest, a centre upon which the bent of our minds is turned.

So the Lord speaks to Saul of Tarsus and announces Himself; He says, “But rise up and stand on thy feet”. Now that is the point that made me turn to this scripture, this very interesting word of the Lord to Saul of Tarsus, “But rise up and stand on thy feet”. Saul must have felt very humbled to think that he had persecuted this glorious Person who had spoken to him in such words of manifest grace. How humiliated he must have felt to realise that this same Jesus, who had been the objective, perhaps a few moments before, of the utmost hatred on his part, was speaking to him in grace. The Lord says to him, “Stand on thy feet”; that is to remind us, I have no doubt, of the glorious efficacy and completeness of the work of Jesus, that everything has been done that our guilt might be purged, that we might stand cleared of guilt in God’s presence, and that we may know what it is to put on Christ, to get free of the power of flesh in the light of God’s condemnation of sin in the flesh in the cross of Jesus.

Think of that shed blood; think of what John presents—the smiting of His side, the flowing forth of the blood and of the water. There is not only that which purges guilt—the blood—but the water, that which meets the need of moral cleansing, the cleansing by the Spirit through the word, that we may come suitably into God’s presence. All is effected in the dying and raising of Jesus. The Lord can say to such a man, “Stand on thy feet”. Saul might have said,

‘What about my history?’. The word would be that that is finished. The Lord would intimate that that would never come before Him again, never, and that it had been judged in His death, so He can say to Saul of Tarsus, “Stand on thy feet”. It would take some time perhaps for this dear man to arrive at what had taken place and to

understand the truth of what I have lightly touched on, but the point is that the Lord can say this to the man, “Stand on thy feet”, because of this wonderful provision from God’s side in Christ, provision which is perfectly adapted to a man’s needs, whatever kind of man he is, to bring him into God’s presence fit to be there, and not only fit to be there, but fit to be used in the course of His interests here.

“Rise up and stand on thy feet”. What a word that is to us! Let other things be done with. Let the things that belong to this time of the Spirit govern each one of us; let us be in the free gain of all that Christ has effected in the sacrificial work in love and power that He has undertaken. Let trivial things, which Satan seeks to bring in to despoil us of what is so great, be cast aside.

This dear man was brought round to see things as God sees them. He yearned for what God yearns for, to see the assembly secured for Christ, and he laboured that what belongs to the assembly might be secured in the places he visited. What a labourer he was! He was not negligent of God and His claims, the claims of His grace upon men, but came round to God’s side to see them, and laboured at them. So the word is, “For, for this purpose have I appeared to thee, to appoint thee to be a servant and a witness both of what thou hast seen, and of what I shall appear to thee in”—remarkable words, as if the Lord is saying to Saul of Tarsus, ‘I am going to maintain active relations with you. This is not the last disclosure you will receive from Me; there will be more yet’. The Lord is just showing that He is going to keep this man in relation with Him as a channel for God’s blessing. When we think of where Christ is, and the character of the operation of His power and His grace, and the kind of results
that He is able to secure in men, we can only say, what a wonderful time this is!

I just had the concern that we come into the gain of this. This was a vision from heaven to Saul of Tarsus; it—was imperative that he answer to it. But, you know, the truth of God is brought to bear upon us in its imperative character. The grace of the Lord Jesus is wonderfully manifest in this episode; and the grace of the Lord Jesus is available to you. But do not miss what belongs to this remarkable time of the Spirit! The knowledge of our God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit involves the wealth which He has brought in in the introduction and maintaining of the truth. ‘Come into these things’, He would say; ‘come right in; the power is there in Christ in glory and in the Spirit in the assembly’. Here is a man who had been embittered to the point of such active attack against Christ and His interests, but who was told by that same glorious Lord to stand on his feet. That word would come to us, dear brethren; do not hold back! Many things the enemy would use to hold us back; he would engage us with ourselves, with our frailties, with our histories, but the word is, “Rise up and stand on thy feet”, because this is the great time of an exalted Christ and of the Spirit here.
There is resource to effect things in the souls of men answering to Christ and answering to God’s great thoughts in the assembly.

But now this man is to become a leader. He is to pursue a course of service; that is to say, not only has the Lord secured him, but He takes him up in distinctive activity. This again is the mark of this wonderful time; He does not just secure persons and isolate them. He would say, ‘Come right into the flow, the rich flow of all that is transpiring in this wonderful time’. So he takes matters up in

such thoroughness as to Christ and His interests. Saul of Tarsus’s total committal to the interests of Christ comes in here. We see that from God’s side all is presented glorious; Christ is on high, His work complete, and the efficacy of His work is presented to men; the gift of the Spirit too is presented as God’s thought for men, the activities of the Spirit engaging the hearts of His lovers with Jesus and God’s pleasure in Him as Man. The great divine objective in mind here is the assembly, of which the Lord could say, “On this rock I will build my assembly” (Matthew 16: 18); that is what is to bring out the greatness of Christ—the assembly is being built. But will you not come into the working out of it? I would say to myself, ‘Shall I not come into this?’.

The consequence of the way in which the Lord speaks to this man is to secure him as an active servant for His interests; he does not hold back, nor does he suffer any holding back on the part of others with whom he has to do, such as his beloved child Timothy. It is the time, you see, to come into these things. There is to be the answer on our side, just as there was an answer on the side of Saul of Tarsus as he went forward, under the Lord’s direction, and became so quickly and so remarkably effective in His interests. The scale of operations was not small. Take a look at a map of Europe and see how widely Saul, later Paul, ranged in his service, those four missionary journeys embracing pretty much the whole of the habitable world at the time at which they took place. Think of the energy, the ceaseless energy, of this man! Remember the conditions in which he laboured; yet he laboured on and let nothing stand in his way of continuing committal to the labour that the Lord had opened up to him. There is to be a clear answer to Christ right the way through this time of the Spirit in something of this quality.

So Paul had one chosen by him at a critical time who was singularly the subject of his affection and attention and care, that is Timotheus. He writes him two letters, as we well know, two epistles to sustain that younger man in the course of the testimony in a dark day, showing us that God has provided for the darkest day. He has made provision. It is as if He would say, ‘I am equal to the testimony in its widest extent, and I am equal to it in smaller circumstances, and I will show the quality of what I can do in small circumstances in these closing moments’. So Timothy, setting before us one who moved in dark times, is instructed in these things. It is not for me in a time like this to go into the teaching of the letters, but rather to emphasize the character of them. The beloved apostle is passing things on to Timothy as his beloved child. What times they must have had together! What a close link there was, but that link worked out in the continuance of the testimony.

Dear brethren, the continuance of the testimony is very much the challenge of the moment, and God has made provision in power that it may continue. The basis and character of continuance is unfolded to Timothy by the beloved apostle, who shows him that in the midst of breakdown God has made a way through. In the midst of broken conditions there is a way in which the testimony shall be fittingly maintained for God, a way in which there shall yet bean expression under God’s eye of what is precious to Him in the assembly. All this enters into the Pauline instruction to Timothy; and it enters into the Pauline instruction to us.

So he addresses himself, near the end of this closing word, to his beloved child, “Fill up the full measure of thy ministry. For I am already being poured out, and the time of my release is come. I have combated the good combat, I have finished the race”, referring back to the time of his active service. It is as if he says, ‘Timothy, the continuance depends on you’. That is the word for us at this time; this time of the Spirit continues in all the glory of it, the divine resource from His side in no sense changed. Christ in glory is the same, every resource in His hand as it ever was; the Spirit is here and His power and the grace of His activity are unchangeable. How shall we, according to our several links with Christ and with the Spirit, move through for the continuance of the testimony? The word is very clear to Timothy in this chapter, and indeed in this whole second epistle; Paul is about to depart, but is the testimony to cease when Paul is removed from it? Let us ask ourselves today in our several circumstances—is the testimony to cease? Let it be the resolve of every one of us that it shall continue, as in view of the moment when He, once spurned, rejected, and crucified, comes in glory to take up His rights here.

In the meantime He has those who love Him, who stand in His rights and cherish the preciousness of the One whose rights they are. Let there be no slipping back! Let there be no failing! Let there be no half-hearted standing in things to which such glory belongs! Let us see that we go through, dear brethren, in unreserved committal to Christ and His glory. Just as in Pauline times, the testimony and its continuance depend upon the faithfulness of younger men. The resources of this dispensation in Christ and in the Spirit are unchangingly available to carry through what is of God in changed persons, to bring in something that is fresh and powerful in view of God securing His great end. Let our courage
and confidence in God not fail in view of the great end that is before us when the Lord Jesus appears. Let us be marked off as those who love Him and His appearing, for His name’s sake.

There is a moral history preceding this statement, “I dwell among mine own people”. Men generally do not reckon in this way for they are always aspiring to reach a higher stratum of society. For instance, it would be esteemed a very great favour to be invited by the Queen to her palace; then as we come down the scale there are titled persons such as lords and knights, and some may have a strong desire to be associated with them. But this woman, who had shown such alacrity in respect of Jehovah’s servant Elisha, said, when asked, “Wouldest thou be spoken for to the king, or to the captain of the host?”—“I dwell among mine own people”.
Who would compare the outward status of earth’s so-called ‘high society’ with the secret joy of companionship with lowly persons who are heaven’s aristocracy?

Now, dear brethren, all this comes as a challenge to us and I would raise the question with each one—Are we content in a world marked by increasing discontent? Paul in 1 Timothy 6: 6 states that “Piety with contentment is great gain”. As we bring God into every one of our circumstances we experience the great gain of contentment, and this wealthy, or it could read ‘great’, woman was characterised by this feature in her links with company which could not be surpassed.

This is a very instructive chapter. The first section, 2 Kings 4: 1–7, corresponds with individual exercise outlined in the Epistle to the Romans; verses 32–37, where the son is received from the dead again, would link with Colossians; and the man from Baal-shalishah in verses 42–44 would correspond with Ephesian truth in that he comes from a heavenly clime and country.

The chapter begins with death and debt and the dire threat of slavery, and the first section ends by showing the illimitable resources which are available as full room is made for the Spirit of God, suggested in the oil. Elisha asks in verse 2, “Tell me, what hast thou in the house?”. What a word for us, beloved brethren. What have we by way of spiritual resources, that which we can appropriate as our own? The woman replies, “Thy handmaid has not anything at all in the house but a pot of oil”, as if the pot of oil was an afterthought and scarcely worthy of mention. Many believers require light regarding the Spirit and need instruction as to how to make use of the Spirit of God dwelling in us. In Romans 8 the believer is “in Christ Jesus”, and the Spirit of God dwells and operates in him; in place of death the Spirit is “life on account of righteousness” (Romans 8: 10); instead of debt “the righteous requirement of the law” is “fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to flesh but according to Spirit” (verse 4); and in contrast to slavery, we read in verses 14 and 15, “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God. For ye have not received a spirit of bondage again for fear, but ye have received a spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father”.

To arrive at all this, the woman had to go through some measure of exercise in borrowing empty vessels, shutting the door upon herself and her sons and pouring out the oil into all the vessels, in regard to which Elisha says, “Let it not be few”. When she says, “Bring me yet a vessel”, she seemed to reach the idea that limitation was in the vessels and not in the Spirit of God for, when there was not a vessel more, we read, “And the oil stayed”.

It is a definite landmark in our spiritual career when we realise consciously that the Spirit of God dwells in us for power and thus renders us independent of anything that worldly streams may offer, and that He is the source of present satisfaction as the Lord states in John 4, “The water which I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water, springing up into eternal life” (John 4: 14). The prophet then instructs her to “Go, sell the oil, and pay thy debt, and live thou and thy sons on the rest”—and there is no cessation to “the rest”.

Morally the wealthy, or ‘great’, woman mentioned in verse 8 is the same person who was in spiritual affluence as living, she and her sons, on the rest. She perceives that Elisha is a holy man of God and proposes to her husband that they should make a small upper chamber with walls for the man of God and provide a bed, a table, a seat and a lampstand. We might think that the room was sparsely furnished, but she saw to it that every requisite was available for the man of God; the bed to enable him to have rest in view of further service, the table for the enjoyment of fellowship, the seat in order that he might meditate on the great things of God, and lastly the lampstand that fresh light from God might be continually imparted.

Elisha says to Gehazi his servant, “Call this Shunammite. And he called her, and she stood before him. And he said to him, Say now to her. Behold, thou hast been careful for us with all this care; what is to be done for thee? wouldest thou be spoken for to the king, or to the captain of the host? And she said, I dwell among mine own people”. She must have had a very enlarged appreciation of her own people in that the suggested honourable mention of her to the king or to the captain of the host had no appeal. Her “own people” were of such value to her that she was just delighted to dwell among them.

You will see, therefore, how she arrives in moral history at such an appreciation of the saints of God, and I have an impression, beloved brethren, that in the measure in which there is full room made in us for the Spirit of God there will not only be “piety with contentment” but there will be unfeigned love for one another and holy joy experienced in dwelling among our own people.

Some of us here belong to small companies and in one way it is almost an asset to be in a small meeting where each is known to the other in a more intimate way than in a large company and there is thus more opportunity for love to express itself personally. I trust that the brethren, therefore, may be encouraged. Oh what it is to be sufficiently near the Lord Jesus to gain an impression of what the saints are to Him for His own heart’s delight and also what they are to the “God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory”, as we read in Ephesians 1: 17, “what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints”. The Holy Spirit of God is with and in us to lead us into a fuller understanding of these things and may we desire increasingly to have the divine viewpoint of the people of God. In Psalm 137 the writer in verses 5 and 6 says, “If I forget thee, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill; If I do not remember thee, let my tongue cleave to my palate—if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy”. Might I ask, wherein does our joy lie? What supreme delight is connected with Christ and His assembly, and as we are committed to His chief interest on earth we shall be able, like this wealthy woman, to state, “I dwell among mine own people”.

Deuteronomy 32: 11, 12; Genesis 45: 25–28; 46: 1; 24: 54–I wish to say a few words about transport. The first passage we have read would apply especially to the young, then we read of an old man, and finally about a maiden.

Boaz speaks to Ruth as to her having taken refuge under the wings of Jehovah the God of Israel (Ruth 2: 12), and the passage in Deuteronomy, speaking of God’s care for His people, refers to the wings of an eagle. To encourage the young birds to leave, the mother bird removes the inner lining of the nest, making it uncomfortable. The eaglets might need courage also to leave the nest, and maybe the Spirit is urging us now to make the attempt.

The Lord said to Peter, “Draw out into the deep water”, Luke 5: 4. We need to ‘cut our moorings’ and move out. We come to meetings like this—some of us have been coming to meetings most of our lives but what is the effect? Does it give us a fresh urge to move? Has it done something spiritually in us? The Spirit would urge us to move out into the heavenly realm now. These eaglets would wish to fly—they have been furnished with wings to do so and would not enjoy their life properly if they did not—but they must make the first attempt to do so. In the same way bathing is not properly enjoyed until one can swim.

The little eagle might fear that it would not be able to fly and that it would fall from that great height. It must make the attempt. The scripture says, “As the eagle stirreth up its nest, hovering over its young, spreadeth out its wings, taketh them, beareth them on its feathers, so Jehovah alone did lead him, and no strange god was with him”. If the eaglet should fall the mother bird would swoop down and take it on her powerful wings. Exodus 19: 4 refers to this; God says there, “Ye have seen … how I have borne you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself”.

If I do move out, God’s affectionate care for me is sure. It means that in spirit I leave natural and material things to find my life in the spiritual realm. An eagle, having found its wings, must delight in soaring in the heavens. The writer in Proverbs 30: 19 refers to the way of an eagle in the heavens as one of the things too wonderful for him. An eagle can draw over its eyes a third eyelid and is thus able to go directly through a storm. So the power of the Holy Spirit is sufficient to bring us through any storm. Trust yourself to those powerful wings and He will transport you to where Christ is.

The passage in Genesis 45 indicates a different mode of transport. We find in Jacob an old and discouraged man. There are those like him today. Their discouragement has led them to do nothing. For Jacob, when Joseph had gone, everything had gone, but when the light came to him that “Joseph is still alive” it says, “his heart fainted, for he did not believe them”. We were speaking in the previous meeting as to faith being light as to facts received in the heart, and the Spirit enables me to make it my own. The fact is that our Joseph is alive—a living Man at the right hand of God raised from the dead, ascended, and glorified. However, when Jacob saw the waggons that Joseph had sent to carry him, his spirit revived. The true Joseph has sent all the transport that is required to bring you in spirit now to where He is. The Holy Spirit is power to carry us into a sphere of light and love and liberty. Looking on the glory of the Lord we are transformed according to the same image from glory to glory (2 Corinthians 3: 18). By the Spirit we behold the face of our Moses, the Lord Jesus, and thus take on that glory.

Now Jacob receives the light and moves in relation to it. It was not only that he said, “I will go”, but he takes his journey to the source from which the waggons came. Merely saying, ‘I will go’ is not sufficient. Deborah tells us that “in the divisions of Reuben there were great resolves of heart”, but they abode among the sheep-folds (Judges 5: 15, 16). Israel took his journey with all that he had and came to Beer-sheba—the well of the oath. We can count on divine promises as moving in obedience to the light in the power of the Holy Spirit.

Genesis 24 is a beautiful type of the assembly being carried over to the heavenly Man as a present experience. She must state her decision. “Let us call the maiden and inquire at her mouth”. She is asked, “Wilt thou go with this man? And she said, will go”. The man would represent the Holy Spirit—He has adequate power for the journey. Let us go, with His guidance, to the heavenly sphere where Christ is to find now our life with Him there.

However, the first step has to be taken. If a diver stops at the end of the spring-board to see how far down it is, he is unlikely to take the plunge. “Wilt thou go with this man? And she said, I will go”. As we thus commit ourselves God will not deprive us of anything that would be for our good, but we must keep the goal before us—one object, the Lord Jesus—each step of the journey. I do not think Rebecca found the journey very long. She would be like Paul, who kept the goal before him (Philippians 3: 13, 14).

In closing I refer to the wings of a dove (see Psalm 55: 6). The Lord speaks of the wings of a hen as protective and we have had before us the wings of an eagle as strength, but the dove is a homing bird. If you bring it far from its cote it will find its way straight home. The Holy Spirit here will bring us now in our spirits back to the place from which He came—Christ in glory. Let us use those wings. May the Lord bless the word.
Assembled now with joy to celebrate
Thy holy Supper, Lord on Thee we wait,
That such unfathomable love may find
Response that shall refresh Thy longing mind.
Whilst Thou art absent from this world is set
Thy Supper and we prove the love that met
And vanquished Satan’s power. As Thy freed men
Thy death we show till Thou shalt come again.
Thy perfect love that could despise the shame
Of Calvary’s death will now its answer claim
In joy from those who know its greatest wealth,
For Thou for us deliv’redst up Thyself.
That mighty love, in constancy unmatched,
Chose thus to prove itself to one attached
By purposes divine and heavenly kin—
Though still on earth—and meet response to win.
London

‘MY SISTER’ OR ‘MY WIFE’? When Abram went down to Egypt in Genesis 12 (and it happened again in chapter 20), he adopted the device of saying that Sarah, his wife, was his sister. If, moving in our own wisdom, we go down to Egypt, that is sure to happen. I shall begin to put my personal interests, my business, or my home and family, in the first place, “and the assembly will take some lower place. But just as a man’s wife (speaking of what, is natural) has the first place in his affections and arrangements; so the assembly is to take priority, with us. It is a sure sign of spiritual decline when the assembly slips in our order of priorities. She is still my sister; there still some relationship; I still break bread; I still love the brethren; but other things are becoming more important. I find, for example, more and more reasons for not being at the meetings. Other interests eat into the time that I used to devote to the things of the Lord. The assembly is my sister, but no longer my wife. May the Lord awaken us to this danger. Let His love afresh constrain us. He loved the assembly and delivered Himself up for it. To purchase it He sold “all whatever he had”. He never regards her in any lesser light than as His wife. May our affection and devotion take on something of that sacrificial character.

paragraphs.speaker: ARS
paragraphs.text: I suppose a godly sister can give a brother who is in the work very good advice sometimes, would you not think?

paragraphs.speaker: JT
paragraphs.text: I know it to be so. What is to be discerned is that sisters have excellent instincts, better than men have; hence the importance of listening to their advice and of taking them into our confidence.
